wine.name: Pétrus
wine.grapes: Merlot, effectively the whole blend; older vintages could carry a small share of Cabernet Franc.
wine.sites: One vineyard at the high point of the Pomerol plateau, on a buttonhole of dense, iron rich blue clay, a smectite that swells when wet, holds back water and makes the roots work hard.
wine.making: The grapes are picked in the afternoons, once the morning dew has dried. The wine is fermented in concrete vats and aged for eighteen to twenty months in oak barrels, about half of them new in most accounts, before it is bottled at the estate.
wine.glass: Black plum, black cherry and truffle over cocoa and a note of iron, with liquorice and violet; dense and velvety, with ripe, fine tannin and a long, warm, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Supple enough to taste young, it then closes and needs fifteen to twenty years in a strong vintage; the great years last half a century.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two and an old one gently off its sediment; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The estate's name alone, with no Château before it, under an image of Saint Peter holding the keys of heaven.
The appellation of the clay and gravel plateau beside Libourne, which has never been classified.

records.table: Almost pure Merlot from a buttonhole of blue clay at the top of the Pomerol plateau, Pétrus carries no classification at all. It is plum, truffle and velvet, and needs years in bottle before it opens.
records.story: At the Universal Exhibition in Paris in 1878 a Pomerol wine won a gold medal, an early sign of fame for a commune the brokers of 1855 had passed over: Pétrus, then the property of the Arnaud family; its name is the Latin for Peter. From the mid 1920s Madame Loubat, who kept a hotel in Libourne and died in 1961, bought shares in the estate, and by the 1940s she held all of it and had given it the label that shows Saint Peter holding the keys of heaven. In the same decade she gave the Libourne merchant Jean-Pierre Moueix (1913 to 2003) the sole right to sell the wine, and the 1947 is a vintage of history. When the frost of 1956 killed vines across the Right Bank, she had the estate's vines cut back to grow again from their old roots rather than pulled up and replanted, and so kept their age. In 1964 the Moueix family bought a share from her heirs, and around 1970 a parcel bought from neighbouring Château Gazin joined the vineyard. Pomerol never drew up a ranking, and Pétrus has never needed one: its standing rests on the clay, the Merlot and the care of one family of merchants.

others.name: La Fleur-Pétrus
others.note: A separate estate on the Pomerol plateau, long run by the Moueix house of Libourne; a different wine, not a second wine of Pétrus.

traps: Pétrus holds no classification: Pomerol has never been ranked, so a list that calls it a first growth is wrong.
The label reads Pétrus alone; there is no Château before the name.
Pétrus makes no second wine: La Fleur-Pétrus and Trotanoy are separate Pomerol estates, not lesser bottlings of it.

questions.exp: Pétrus is effectively all Merlot from blue clay; near equal Cabernet Franc and Merlot is Cheval Blanc, and a third each of three grapes is Figeac.

questions.exp: Madame Loubat bought her first shares in the 1920s and held Pétrus until her death in 1961; the other three widows ran Champagne houses.

wine.name: Le Pin
wine.grapes: Merlot, all or nearly all of it, with a trace of Cabernet Franc in some years.
wine.sites: A small vineyard of gravel and clay on the Pomerol plateau, beside Vieux Château Certan, around the house where a pine tree gave the estate its name.
wine.making: Fermented in small stainless steel vats, the wine is run into oak barrels, most or all of them new, for its malolactic fermentation, and stays in them for fourteen to eighteen months before it is bottled at the estate.
wine.glass: Ripe plum, black cherry and mocha over cream, vanilla and a little truffle; plush and round, with soft, sweet tannin, gentle acidity and a long, rich finish.
wine.ageing: Open and generous within a few years of the vintage, it keeps its charm for twenty years and more in a strong year.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one only to take it off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The estate's name, from a pine tree that stood beside the house on the plot.
The appellation of the plateau north east of Libourne, which has no classification of any kind.

records.table: Begun by a Belgian family in 1979, Le Pin is Pomerol Merlot from a few rows of gravel and clay, raised mostly in new oak. Plush and openly ripe, with plum, mocha and cream, it charms far younger than its neighbours.
records.story: A pine tree beside a modest house gave Le Pin its name. The Thienpont family, wine merchants from Belgium, had owned Vieux Château Certan on the Pomerol plateau since 1924, and in 1979 members of the family bought this small plot nearby, with its house and a small cellar. The first vintage was made that autumn in those rough surroundings and raised in old barrels from Vieux Château Certan; malolactic fermentation in barrel, begun when there were too few vats, became a habit of the house. The early vintages sold slowly, but the 1982 was praised by critics and made the estate's name. From 1991, when Valandraud in Saint-Émilion made its first vintage, a wave of tiny, dense, new oaked wines from sheds and garages followed; their makers were called garagistes, and Le Pin was named as their forerunner. The estate stayed small and never sought a rank: Pomerol has no classification. In 2011 a new cellar designed by Belgian architects opened on the site. Le Pin stands for the opulent side of Pomerol, the wine to pour when a guest wants pleasure young rather than in twenty years.

others.name: Vieux Château Certan
others.note: The neighbouring estate of the wider Thienpont family since 1924, made apart from Le Pin; a different wine, not its second.

traps: Le Pin has no classification: Pomerol has never been ranked, so its fame rests on the wine alone.
Le Pin and Vieux Château Certan share a family name but are separate estates with separate wines.
Le Pin is Pomerol, not Saint-Émilion, though most of the garage wines it inspired were made in Saint-Émilion.

Large old casks for three years

questions.exp: Le Pin goes into oak barrels, most or all of them new, for its malolactic fermentation and ageing; large old casks or bare concrete would give none of that mocha and cream.

wine.name: Château Cheval Blanc
wine.classification: Premier Grand Cru Classé A from 1955 until it withdrew in 2021
wine.grapes: Cabernet Franc and Merlot in near equal parts, the Cabernet Franc a little more of the vineyard, with a touch of Cabernet Sauvignon in some years.
wine.sites: Gravel, clay and sand side by side in the far north west of Saint-Émilion, hard against the Pomerol border, on land bought out of Figeac from 1832.
wine.making: Each parcel is fermented apart in a concrete vat sized to it, in the cellar that opened among the vines in June 2011. The wine is then aged for sixteen to eighteen months in oak barrels, which the estate replaces every year, and bottled at the château.
wine.glass: Violet, red plum and raspberry over sweet tobacco, mint and cedar, with truffle as it ages; silky and perfumed, with fine, satin tannin and a long, fresh finish.
wine.ageing: Charming in its first years, it then closes and opens again after fifteen or so; the great vintages last half a century and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The appellation, the stricter of Saint-Émilion's two; it is not a rank in the classification.
The rank printed on older vintages, before the estate left the classification in 2021.

records.table: Château Cheval Blanc is the Saint-Émilion estate on the Pomerol border where Cabernet Franc stands beside Merlot in near equal parts on gravel, clay and sand. It pours violets, red plum and silken tannin, perfume before power, and its 1947 is a vintage of history.
records.story: The land of Cheval Blanc was once part of Château Figeac. In 1832 a judge of Libourne bought the heart of it, and more Figeac land followed over the next two decades. Through his daughter's marriage of 1852 it passed to the Laussac-Fourcaud family, later the Fourcaud-Laussac family, who held it until 1998; how it came by its name is not known for certain. It won a medal at the Universal Exhibition in London in 1862, which its label has carried ever since, and a gold medal at Paris in 1878. The 1947, made after an abnormally hot, dry summer, came out so ripe and dense that it is a vintage of history, talked of for its weight as a wine almost like Port. When Saint-Émilion drew up its first classification in 1955, Cheval Blanc and Ausone were the two estates ranked Premier Grand Cru Classé A, a rank they held alone until 2012. In June 2011 a new cellar of concrete vats, sized to the parcels, opened among the vines. In 2021 Cheval Blanc withdrew from the classification, as Ausone did, objecting to the weight its criteria gave to matters beyond the wine in the glass. When a guest doubts that Cabernet Franc can lead on the Right Bank, Cheval Blanc is the bottle to pour.

others.name: Le Petit Cheval
others.note: The second wine, Cabernet Franc and Merlot from the same vineyard.

others.name: Cheval des Andes
others.note: A Malbec led red of Mendoza, made with Terrazas de los Andes since the 1999 vintage.

traps: Cheval Blanc and Figeac share gravel and a history but are separate estates: Cheval Blanc's land was carved from Figeac.
Cheval Blanc left the Saint-Émilion classification in 2021 and holds no rank in the classification of 2022, though older bottles print Premier Grand Cru Classé.
Cheval Blanc is Saint-Émilion, not Pomerol, though its vines run to the Pomerol border.

questions.exp: Ausone also withdrew in 2021, by its own decision, and Angélus followed early in 2022; Figeac and Pavie became the two A estates of 2022, and Pétrus, in Pomerol, was never classified.

wine.name: Château Ausone
wine.classification: Premier Grand Cru Classé A from 1955 until it withdrew in 2021
wine.grapes: Cabernet Franc and Merlot, the Cabernet Franc usually the larger share, from an even split to about two thirds of the blend.
wine.sites: A south east facing amphitheatre on the limestone côte directly below the town, with cellars in old quarry galleries beneath the château.
wine.making: Each block is fermented apart in oak vats after a cold soak. The wine then goes into barrels, new or nearly all new, for its malolactic fermentation and some twenty months of ageing in the cellars cut into the rock, before it is bottled at the château.
wine.glass: Crushed stone, blood orange and red cherry over violet, black tea and clove, cool and tightly wound; firm, fine grained tannin, high acidity and a long, chalky finish.
wine.ageing: Austere and closed when young, it needs twenty years in a strong vintage and can go on for many decades after.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for two hours, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Named for the Latin poet Ausonius, whose villa, by local belief, stood on this slope.

records.table: Named for the Roman poet Ausonius, Château Ausone grows on the limestone slope beneath the town of Saint-Émilion. Cabernet Franc with Merlot, it is cool, stony and tightly wound, a wine for the long cellar.
records.story: Ausonius (about 310 to about 395), the Latin poet of Bordeaux, tutor to the future emperor Gratian and the poet of the vines of the Moselle, gave the estate its name: local belief long held that his villa stood on this slope below the town, though no one has proved it. The vines grow on the limestone côte in an amphitheatre beneath the château, and the cellars run back into old quarry galleries cut into the rock. When Saint-Émilion drew up its first classification in 1955, Ausone and Cheval Blanc were the two estates ranked Premier Grand Cru Classé A, a pair that held that rank alone for more than half a century. For much of that time two families shared the estate, and a long dispute between them, which went to the courts, ended in the mid 1990s, when the Vauthier family bought the other half and took sole charge of vineyard and cellar. Ausone kept its A rank in 2012, when Angélus and Pavie were raised to join it, but in 2021 it withdrew from the classification, as Cheval Blanc did. Ausone is the voice of the limestone: cool, slow and built for the cellar, the opposite pole to Cheval Blanc's gravel.

others.name: Chapelle d'Ausone
others.note: The second wine, Cabernet Franc and Merlot from the same slope.

traps: Ausone is limestone côte and Cheval Blanc is gravel beside Pomerol: the two A estates of 1955 differ in soil and in style.

wine.name: Château Figeac
wine.classification: Premier Grand Cru Classé A in the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification
wine.grapes: Roughly a third each of Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Merlot, a share of Cabernet Sauvignon rare on the Right Bank.
wine.sites: Three rises of deep, ancient gravel with flint and quartz over blue clay, in the north west of Saint-Émilion beside Cheval Blanc and the Pomerol border; the gravel ripens both Cabernets.
wine.making: Each parcel is fermented apart in steel or oak vats, and the malolactic fermentation takes place in barrel. The wine is then aged for fifteen to eighteen months in new oak barrels before it is bottled at the château.
wine.glass: Blackcurrant leaf, cedar and graphite over red cherry, tobacco and a little mint, cooler and more structured than most Saint-Émilion; firm, fine tannin, fresh acidity and a long, dry finish.
wine.ageing: Reserved in youth, it opens after ten to fifteen years, and the strong vintages hold for decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two and an old one off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The rank on the label; in 2022 Figeac was placed in its upper group, A.
The appellation, a stricter tier than plain Saint-Émilion and separate from the classification.

records.table: With about a third of Cabernet Sauvignon on gravel beside Cheval Blanc, Château Figeac tastes closer to the Médoc than its neighbours do: blackcurrant leaf, cedar and graphite. In 2022 it was raised to Premier Grand Cru Classé A.
records.story: The estate carries, the story goes, the name of a Gallo-Roman landowner, Figeacus, whose villa stood here in the second century. In the eighteenth century Figeac reached across much of the north west of Saint-Émilion, and in the nineteenth its owners sold land, among it, from 1832, the parcels that became Cheval Blanc. In 1892 the grandparents of Thierry Manoncourt (1917 to 2010) bought the estate, and he took charge of it in 1947, as the estate tells it. He widened the plantings of Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc on the warm gravel and set the blend at about a third of each grape, so that Figeac grew into the Right Bank's Cabernet estate, closer in taste to the Médoc than to its Merlot neighbours. In 1955 it was ranked Premier Grand Cru Classé in Saint-Émilion's first classification, in the group below Ausone and Cheval Blanc, and it stayed in that group through every revision for more than sixty years. In 2022, with Ausone, Cheval Blanc and Angélus gone from the list, Figeac was promoted to A beside Pavie. Offer it to a guest who loves Pauillac: three grapes in near equal parts, cedar before plum.

traps: Figeac and Cheval Blanc share gravel and a history but are different estates: Cheval Blanc's land was carved from Figeac.
Figeac's blend carries about a third of Cabernet Sauvignon, so do not sell it as a Merlot wine.
Figeac was raised to A only in 2022, when Pavie, A since 2012, was the one other estate in the rank.

report: Rechecked with search on 12 November 2026 in six searches, one of them empty, and two shared with Cheval Blanc and Ausone: the estate's own pages give the purchase of 1892 by Thierry Manoncourt's grandparents, his taking charge in 1947, his death in 2010, the blend in thirds and the three gravel rises over blue clay.

Thierry Manoncourt's birth in 1917 rests on Wikipedia and on Decanter's obituary, which gives his age at death as 92; Decanter dates his taking charge to 1946 and a French trade report his first harvest to 1943, so the year is the estate's own and hedged.
His training as an agronomist was not confirmed, the agricultural engineer of the 1890s accounts being another man, and is cut.

The order of picking, Merlot first, was not confirmed and is cut; the steel and oak vats, the malolactic in barrel and fifteen to eighteen months in new oak rest on the search, with up to twenty months in one account.
The family's present members are living and are not named.

changed: sites: three rises of deep, ancient gravel with flint and quartz over blue clay, by the estate's own page, where the record said three low rises of deep gravel that warm quickly.

making: steel or oak vats, malolactic in barrel and fifteen to eighteen months in new oak (Decanter's profile, sommelier-academy), where the record said the Merlot is picked first and well over a year in new oak; the order of picking is cut, unconfirmed.
story: a Gallo-Roman landowner, Figeacus, as the story goes, where the record said a Gallo-Roman family; the eighteenth century estate across much of the north west stands on two accounts.

story: bought in 1892 by Thierry Manoncourt's grandparents, by the estate, where the record said by his family; his years 1917 to 2010 (Wikipedia, Decanter) and his taking charge in 1947 as the estate tells it; his training as an agronomist is cut, unconfirmed.
story: he set the blend at about a third of each grape (the estate) and widened the Cabernets (Decanter's obituary); the B group of 1955 and the A of 2022 beside Pavie (Berry Bros, Decanter).
others: Petit-Figeac has been the second wine since the 2012 vintage and was La Grange Neuve de Figeac before it (the search), where the record said only that it is made in Figeac's cellar.
